source_text: Contra hoc dictum est iniusta quidem esse nunc ista, non tamen mala, et ideo iniusta, quia contra leges, quibus prohibentur, fiunt, ideo autem non mala, quia, si mala essent, numquam deo utique placuissent; porro si numquam placuissent, numquam facta essent illo non sinente, qui omnia potest et qui talia non contemneret, quando tam magna sunt, ut contra ipsam religionem, qua deus colitur, fierent, si male fierent. hic ego, si propterea, inquam, mala non sunt, quia deo placere hinc probantur, quod ea fieri sinit omnipotens, quomodo erit bonum, quod fieri prohibentur et euertuntur? si autem hoc bonum non est, quod euertuntur, quae deo placent, hoc fieri non sineret omnipotens, quia et hoc contra religionem fit, qua colitur deus, si ea, quae deo placent, ab hominibus euertuntur. si autem hoc, cum male fiat, permittit omnipotens, non ideo putanda sunt illa bona, quod ea fieri permisit omnipotens.
thought_title: The dilemma of permission and pleasure
orientation: Augustine is answering the interlocutors' objection that the acts God permits must be good because they please him.
pass_a_gloss: Against this [it] has been said [that] unjust indeed [they] are now these [things], not however evil, and therefore unjust, because against [the] laws, by which [they] are forbidden, [they] are done, therefore however not evil, because, if evil [they] were, never to God certainly [they] would have pleased; furthermore if never [they] had pleased, never [they] would have been done [with] him not allowing, who all [things] can and who such [things] not would despise, when so great [they] are, that against [the] very religion, by which God is worshipped, [they] would be done, if evilly [they] were done. here I, if for this reason, [I] say, evil not [they] are, because to God [they] please [and] from this [they] are proved, that them [he] allows to be done [being] omnipotent, how will [it] be good, that [which] [they] are forbidden to be done and [they] are overturned? if however this good not is, that [they] are overturned, which to God please, this [he] would not allow to be done [being] omnipotent, because also this against [the] religion is done, by which is worshipped God, if those [things], which to God please, by men are overturned. if however this, when evilly [it] is done, permits [the] omnipotent, not therefore [they] are to be thought those [things] good, because them [he] permitted to be done [being] omnipotent.

choices.term: iniusta quidem esse nunc ista, non tamen mala
choices.english: these things are indeed unjust now, but not evil
choices.why: Preserves the interlocutors' precise distinction between legal wrongness (iniusta) and moral evil (mala), which is the hinge of the whole argument.
rejected: these things are indeed wrong now, but not bad
these things are indeed unlawful now, but not wicked

choices.english: when he was not allowing it
choices.why: Keeps the ablative absolute's temporal-causal force and the negative participle, showing God's non-permission as the condition.
Literal rendering of the relative clause describing God's omnipotence, matching the brief's emphasis on the Almighty's power to permit or prevent.
rejected: who has power over all things

choices.why: Consistent with the brief's glossary for 'temples and idols' being overthrown; keeps the physical destruction sense.

choices.english: if they were being done evilly
choices.why: Preserves the adverb 'male' (evilly) as distinct from the adjective 'mala' (evil), which the interlocutors' argument depends on.
rejected: if they were being done wickedly

pass_b_english: Against this it was said that these things are indeed unjust now, but not evil. They are unjust because they are done against the laws that forbid them, but they are not evil because, if they were evil, they would never have pleased God. And if they had never pleased him, they would never have happened when he was not allowing it—he who can do all things, and who would not disregard such things when they are so great that they are done against the very religion by which God is worshiped, if they were being done evilly.

At this point I said: If they are not evil for the reason that they are shown to please God by the fact that the Almighty allows them to happen, how will it be good that they are forbidden and overthrown? But if this is not good—that they are overthrown—then the Almighty would not allow it to happen, because this too is done against the religion by which God is worshiped, if the things that please God are overthrown by human beings. But if the Almighty permits this when it is done evilly, then those other things should not be considered good simply because the Almighty permitted them to happen.

last_rejected.quote: he who can do all things, and who would not disregard such things when they are so great that they are done against the very religion by which God is worshiped, if they were being done evilly
last_rejected.source_quote: qui omnia potest et qui talia non contemneret, quando tam magna sunt, ut contra ipsam religionem, qua deus colitur, fierent, si male fierent
last_rejected.why: The conditional 'si male fierent' governs the whole clause: God wouldn't ignore them IF they were done evilly. English makes 'if they were being done evilly' a dangling afterthought, weakening the logical force.
last_rejected.fix: he who can do all things, who would not disregard such great wrongs if they were done evilly—wrongs so great that they are done against the very religion by which God is worshiped.
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly renders si male fierent as conditional governing the clause; placement at end is normal English syntax, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: 'Erit' is future indicative, but in this rhetorical question it expresses impossibility/confusion ('how can it be good?'). 'Will it be' sounds like a genuine future inquiry, not the intended logical absurdity.
last_rejected.ruling: 'How will it be good' is a standard rendering of future indicative in rhetorical questions; no meaning lost or changed.
